value.legal_basis: 20 U.S.C. § 7512 (Native Hawaiian Education Act findings), Pub. L. 89-10, title VI, § 6202, as amended

facts.note: Congress finds Native Hawaiians are 'a distinct and unique indigenous people'; that through the Hawaiian Homes Commission Act Congress 'affirmed the special relationship'; that it does not extend services 'because of their race, but because of their unique status as the indigenous people of a once sovereign nation as to whom the United States has established a trust relationship' (para. 12(B)); and lists statutes evidencing 'the political relationship' (para. 13). The findings call Native Hawaiians a people; they do not designate a tribe.

value.legal_basis: Pub. L. 103-150, 107 Stat. 1510 (Apology Resolution), §§ 1-3

facts.note: Section 1 acknowledges 'the suppression of the inherent sovereignty of the Native Hawaiian people', apologizes for the 1893 overthrow and the deprivation of 'the rights of Native Hawaiians to self-determination', and commits to 'reconciliation between the United States and the Native Hawaiian people'. Section 2 defines 'Native Hawaiian' as any descendant of the aboriginal people who, prior to 1778, occupied and exercised sovereignty in the area that now constitutes the State of Hawaii. Section 3: 'Nothing in this Joint Resolution is intended to serve as a settlement of any claims against the United States.'

value.legal_basis: Hawaiian Homes Commission Act, 1920, Act of July 9, 1921, ch. 42, 42 Stat. 108

facts.note: Defines 'native Hawaiian' as 'any descendant of not less than one-half part of the blood of the races inhabiting the Hawaiian Islands previous to 1778' and sets aside lands for homesteading. 20 U.S.C. § 7512(7)-(8) describes this Act as Congress affirming the special relationship. The source is the 1921 enactment; later amendments not reviewed.

value.legal_basis: Hawaii Admission Act, Pub. L. 86-3, 73 Stat. 4, §§ 4 and 5(f)

facts.note: Section 4 adopts the Hawaiian Homes Commission Act as a compact with the United States, amendable in key respects only with federal consent. Section 5(f) requires ceded lands and their proceeds to be held by the State 'as a public trust' for purposes including 'the betterment of the conditions of native Hawaiians, as defined in the Hawaiian Homes Commission Act', with misuse a breach of trust 'for which suit may be brought by the United States'. 20 U.S.C. § 7512(10)-(11) describes these provisions as reaffirming the trust relationship.

value.title: Procedures for Reestablishing a Formal Government-to-Government Relationship With the Native Hawaiian Community (Department of the Interior final rule; 43 C.F.R. Part 50)

facts.note: A federal regulation, not a document of the community. The rule 'does not attempt to reorganize a Native Hawaiian government or draft its constitution'; it sets the procedure the Secretary would use 'if the Native Hawaiian community forms a unified government' that seeks a relationship (summary). The Secretary will reestablish the relationship 'with only one sovereign Native Hawaiian government' (§ 50.3). A reestablished governing entity would not be eligible for Federal Indian programs unless Congress says so (§ 50.44(d)). Effective 2016-11-14. Recorded under governing-document because the contract has no field for a federal procedural rule.

value.title: 43 CFR Part 50 - Procedures for Reestablishing a Formal Government-to-Government Relationship With the Native Hawaiian Community (current codified text)

facts.note: Codified text of the 2016 rule; source line 81 FR 71318, Oct. 14, 2016, with no later amendments shown.

value.detail: No Native Hawaiian government has a formal government-to-government relationship with the United States. The Department of the Interior's Solicitor wrote that the Department 'has not yet received a request' under 43 C.F.R. Part 50 and that a Native Hawaiian government 'has been lacking since the overthrow of the monarchy'.

facts.note: Opinion M-37083 is listed as 'Under Suspension Review' in the Interior M-Opinions index dated May 2026 (interior-m-opinions-index-2026-05), so its legal conclusions may change. The factual statement about requests is as of 2025-01-16.

value.detail: The Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel stated that in the decade since the 2016 rule 'no Native Hawaiian community has availed itself of this opportunity', and that Native Hawaiian statutes do not confer 'formal federal recognition on any Native Hawaiian political entity, which is why no such entity appears' on the Interior recognition list.

facts.note: The same opinion concludes that a Native Hawaiian-serving education grant program is a racial classification subject to strict scrutiny, and leaves unresolved 'whether Congress may treat the native Hawaiians as it does the Indian tribes' (citing Rice v. Cayetano, 528 U.S. 495 (2000)). This differs from the 2016 rule, in which the Department of the Interior took the position that Congress, through more than 150 statutes, recognized that the Native Hawaiian community 'exists as an Indian tribe within the meaning of the Constitution' while also stating Native Hawaiians 'would not be added to the list' of federally recognized tribes (81 FR 71284 and n.4). Contested; record without a tribal status category.

value.legal_basis: Haw. Rev. Stat. § 10H-1 (Act 195, Session Laws of Hawaii 2011)

facts.note: Text: 'The Native Hawaiian people are hereby recognized as the only indigenous, aboriginal, maoli people of Hawaii.' [L 2011, c 195, pt of §2]. The since date is the Act's date as bracketed in § 10H-3(b). § 10H-8(b) adds that members of the qualified Native Hawaiian roll and their descendants 'shall be acknowledged by the State of Hawaii as the indigenous, aboriginal, maoli population of Hawaii' (hawaii-revised-statutes-10h-8).

value.legal_basis: Haw. Rev. Stat. § 10H-8 (Act 195, Session Laws of Hawaii 2011)

facts.note: Reaffirms the 1959 Admission Act delegation to the State 'to address the conditions of the indigenous, native people of Hawaii' and acknowledges members of the qualified Native Hawaiian roll and descendants as 'the indigenous, aboriginal, maoli population of Hawaii'.

value.legal_basis: Haw. Const. art. XII, §§ 4-7 (Hawaiian Affairs), as added by Const. Con. 1978

facts.note: § 4 holds ceded lands 'as a public trust for native Hawaiians and the general public'; § 5 establishes the Office of Hawaiian Affairs to hold property 'in trust for native Hawaiians and Hawaiians'; § 6 sets the trustees' powers; § 7: 'The State reaffirms and shall protect all rights, customarily and traditionally exercised for subsistence, cultural and religious purposes and possessed by ahupua'a tenants who are descendants of native Hawaiians who inhabited the Hawaiian Islands prior to 1778, subject to the right of the State to regulate such rights.' Art. XII §§ 1-3 adopt the Hawaiian Homes Commission Act. The § 5 provision limiting trustee elections to Hawaiian voters was the subject of Rice v. Cayetano (2000); not reviewed here.

Established by the Hawaii Constitution; holds property in trust for native Hawaiians and Hawaiians. The Native Hawaiian roll commission under Haw. Rev. Stat. § 10H-3 is placed within this office 'for administrative purposes only'.
Defined as 'the agency or department of the State of Hawaii that is responsible for administering the HHCA' (Hawaiian Homes Commission Act).

Established by § 202 of the 1921 Act (then a territorial body); the Act was adopted as state law by Haw. Const. art. XII § 1 and as a compact by Admission Act § 4. Its current placement as head of the Department of Hawaiian Home Lands was not verified in a state statute during this session.

value.name: U.S. Department of the Interior, Office of Native Hawaiian Relations

facts.note: Page: 'formally established by Congress in 2004'; its mission includes implementing 'the special political and legal relationship between the United States and the Native Hawaiian Community' and continuing 'the process of reconciliation'. The Solicitor's opinion M-37083 cites the establishing law as Consolidated Appropriations Act, Pub. L. 108-199, div. H, § 148, 118 Stat. 3, 445 (2004).

value.name: Native Hawaiian Organization Notification List (Department of the Interior)

facts.note: Maintained by the Office of Native Hawaiian Relations as a tool for federal notification and consultation under laws such as the National Environmental Policy Act, the National Historic Preservation Act and the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act. Listed organizations are not governments of the community and were not imported. Solicitor's opinion M-37083 states federal agencies currently engage the community 'through Native Hawaiian organizations who serve as its informal representatives'.

Five-member commission within the Office of Hawaiian Affairs to prepare a roll of qualified Native Hawaiians; § 10H-6 directs its dissolution once the roll is published. Whether it has been dissolved was not checked.
Hawaiian home lands administered under the Hawaiian Homes Commission Act and ceded lands held in public trust for native Hawaiians and the general public. Not reservation land.
'English and Hawaiian shall be the official languages of Hawaii'. Tag haw confirmed in the ISO 639-3 registry (source key iso-639-3-haw); Hawaiian has no ISO 639-1 two-letter code.
The Interior page uses 'nā kānaka maoli' (with the plural article nā). Haw. Rev. Stat. § 10H-1 uses 'maoli' in 'indigenous, aboriginal, maoli people'. Diacritics kept as published.

facts.note: CNMI law and the U.S. Census Bureau spell the name 'Chamorro'. Guam law since P.L. 33-236 (2017) uses 'CHamoru' (guam-code-5-chapter-88). The official_name uses the Guam spelling as the lead asked; consider whether CNMI records should show 'Chamorro'.

Compiler's 2017 note: 'The typography of the word “CHamoru” in this chapter reflects the typography as enacted by P.L. 33-236.' The Guam language commission (Kumisión i Fino' CHamoru) uses this spelling throughout its site.

value.legal_basis: 21 G.C.A. ch. 75 (Chamorro Land Trust Act), § 75101(d), enacted by Guam P.L. 12-226 (Feb. 4, 1975)

facts.note: Defines 'Native Chamorro' as 'any person who became a U.S. citizen by virtue of the authority and enactment of the Organic Act of Guam or descendants of such person' and provides leases of Chamorro homelands to native Chamorros. The commission held its first meeting in March 1993. Compiler note: P.L. 35-112 (Dec. 10, 2020) keeps chapter 75 for leases approved before 2021 and enacted a new chapter 75A for later applications (not reviewed). Justia reproduction of the Compiler of Laws text.

value.legal_basis: 1 G.C.A. ch. 21 (Commission on Decolonization for the Implementation and Exercise of Chamorro Self Determination), §§ 2101-2102, created by Guam P.L. 23-147 and reenacted by P.L. 25-106

facts.note: Defines 'Native Inhabitants of Guam' as 'those persons who became U.S. Citizens by virtue of the authority and enactment of the 1950 Organic Act of Guam and descendants of those persons', and intends a plebiscite of Native Inhabitants on independence, free association or statehood. In Davis v. Guam (9th Cir. 2019) the court held that limiting plebiscite voting to 'Native Inhabitants of Guam' violated the Fifteenth Amendment (davis-v-guam-2019). Justia reproduction (compiler revision 2011); later amendments not checked.

value.legal_basis: 5 G.C.A. ch. 88 (Commission on CHamoru Language and the Teaching of the History and Culture of the Indigenous People of Guam), added by Guam P.L. 33-236

facts.note: Establishes within the government of Guam a commission on the CHamoru language and 'the Indigenous People of Guam'; names I Dipåttamenton I Kaohao Guinahan CHamoru (the Department of Chamoru Affairs) as a member. Justia reproduction of the Compiler of Laws text.

value.legal_basis: Constitution of the Northern Mariana Islands, art. XII §§ 1 and 4 (restrictions on alienation of land; 'persons of Northern Marianas descent'), as amended by House Legislative Initiative 18-1 (2014)

facts.note: § 1: acquisition of permanent and long-term interests in real property 'shall be restricted to persons of Northern Marianas descent'. § 4: a person of Northern Marianas descent is a U.S. citizen or national 'who has at least some degree of Northern Marianas Chamorro or Northern Marianas Carolinian blood or a combination thereof'. Implements Covenant § 805 (cnmi-covenant). Original provision ratified 1977, effective 1978 (exact day not taken from this source). Art. XVIII § 5(c) limits voting on Article XII amendments to persons of Northern Marianas descent; the Ninth Circuit invalidated that limit in Davis v. Commonwealth Election Comm'n, 844 F.3d 1087 (2016), as described in davis-v-guam-2019.

value.legal_basis: Covenant to Establish a Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, § 805, approved by Pub. L. 94-241, 90 Stat. 263 (1976), 48 U.S.C. § 1801 note

facts.note: Federal law approving the Covenant: 'in view of the importance of the ownership of land for the culture and traditions of the people of the Northern Mariana Islands', the CNMI government will (for 25 years after the trusteeship ends) and may thereafter restrict acquisition of long-term land interests 'to persons of Northern Mariana Islands descent'. Recorded as territorial-law because it is the land-restriction basis of the Commonwealth's political union; it is not a tribal recognition.

value.legal_basis: Constitution of the Northern Mariana Islands, art. III § 23 (Resident Executive for Indigenous Affairs), Second Const. Conv. Amend. 22 (1985)

facts.note: Creates an office of resident executive to the governor for indigenous affairs, held by a person of Northern Marianas descent, with duties such as establishing a community foundation 'for the advancement of the indigenous people' and serving as 'an advocate of positions taken by indigenous people'. Covers persons of Northern Marianas descent (Chamorro and Carolinian).

facts.note: 'It shall be the policy of the Government of American Samoa to protect persons of Samoan ancestry against alienation of their lands and the destruction of the Samoan way of life and language, contrary to their best interests.' Legislation may protect 'the lands, customs, culture, and traditional Samoan family organization of persons of Samoan ancestry'; land-alienation law changes need two successive legislatures by two-thirds and the Governor. A 2022 Constitutional Review Committee proposed rewording this section; adoption not checked. Text read through the WebFetch tool.

value.legal_basis: Revised Constitution of American Samoa, art. II §§ 3(d) and 4 (Senators must be registered matai; elected in accordance with Samoan custom by county councils)

facts.note: A Senator must 'be the registered matai of a Samoan family who fulfills his obligations as required by Samoan custom'; Senators 'shall be elected in accordance with Samoan custom by the county councils'. This is the constitutional footing of the matai system in the territorial legislature.

value.legal_basis: A.S.C.A. § 37.0204 (restrictions on alienation of land)

facts.note: Prohibits a matai from alienating communal family lands without the Governor's written approval, and prohibits alienating any lands except freehold lands to a person with 'less than one-half native blood'. FAOLEX reproduction; date of the reproduced text not stated.

log.narrative: Congress describes Native Hawaiians as 'a distinct and unique indigenous people' with whom the United States has a trust relationship, and says services are extended not because of race but because of that status (us-code-20-7512-native-hawaiian-education-findings; apology-resolution-1993). The Department of the Interior's 2016 rule nonetheless states that Native Hawaiians would not be added to the federally recognized tribes list, because Congress provides a separate set of Native Hawaiian programs, and it only sets a procedure the Secretary would use if the community forms a single government (interior-native-hawaiian-final-rule-2016). No such government exists: the Interior Solicitor reported in January 2025 that no request had been received (interior-solicitor-opinion-m-37083), an opinion now under suspension review (interior-m-opinions-index-2026-05), and the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel wrote in December 2025 that no Native Hawaiian political entity has formal federal recognition and that the constitutional status of Native Hawaiian preferences is unresolved (justice-olc-race-based-education-programs-2025). Hawaii law separately recognizes Native Hawaiians as 'the only indigenous, aboriginal, maoli people of Hawaii' and protects traditional and customary rights through the Office of Hawaiian Affairs and art. XII § 7, which are state-law statuses, not tribal recognition (hawaii-revised-statutes-10h-1; hawaii-constitution). In the territories, Indigenous status rests on territorial constitutions and codes tied to land and descent: CNMI's 'persons of Northern Marianas descent' under the Covenant (cnmi-constitution; cnmi-covenant), Guam's 'Native Chamorro' land-trust beneficiaries and 'Native Inhabitants of Guam' (guam-code-21-chapter-75; guam-code-1-chapter-21), and American Samoa's protection of lands, custom and the matai system for persons of Samoan ancestry (american-samoa-revised-constitution). None of these is a federal acknowledgment of a tribe, and federal courts have struck down some descent-based voting limits built on them (davis-v-guam-2019), so each record should cite its exact provision rather than a tribal status category.
